Phrygia
frij'i-ä
n. (an inland region of Asia Minor, divided between the Roman provinces of Asia and Galatia, and traversed repeatedly by Paul)
From Greek Phrugia, an ancient inland district of Asia Minor whose old ethnic name outlived the Roman provincial boundaries drawn across it. Luke uses the popular regional name alongside the administrative ones.

Biblical Definition

Phrygia is the high inland country of Asia Minor, an old people and an old name that the Romans cut in two when they drew their provinces. Phrygians were among the pilgrims who heard the apostles speak in their own tongues at Pentecost — “Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene” (Act 2:10) — so the word reached the region before any missionary did. Paul crossed it three times. On the second journey, “when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia” they were “forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” (Act 16:6), a closing of doors that drove them north and finally to the Macedonian vision and to Europe. On the third journey he returned deliberately, going “over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples” (Act 18:23). The two verses set out the whole rhythm of apostolic labour: the Spirit forbids in one place and sends to another, and the same man comes back later to establish what was planted. Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis all lay in Phrygian country, so the epistle to the Colossians is a letter into this region.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Phrygia; it is an inland region of Asia Minor, afterwards divided between the Roman provinces of Asia and Galatia.

expand to see more

PHRYGIA, n. An interior region of Asia Minor, bounded by Bithynia, Galatia, Lycaonia, Pisidia, Lydia and Mysia.

Under the Romans it was divided, part being annexed to Asia and part to Galatia.

Phrygians were present at Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, and heard the apostles in their own tongue.

Paul passed through the country on his second and third journeys.

Colosse, Laodicea and Hierapolis were cities of Phrygia.

Key Scripture

Act 2:10 — "Phrygia, and Pamphylia, in Egypt, and in the parts of Libya about Cyrene, and strangers of Rome, Jews and proselytes,"

Act 16:6 — "Now when they had gone throughout Phrygia and the region of Galatia, and were forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia,"

Act 18:23 — "And after he had spent some time there, he departed, and went over all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples."

Act 16:9 — "And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us."

Modern Corruption

The Spirit's forbidding is read as circumstance or as a failure of nerve, and guidance is reduced to an inward impression; Scripture presents it as the sovereign direction of a mission by its Lord.

expand to see more

Luke says the Holy Ghost forbade them, and the Spirit of Jesus “suffered them not” (Act 16:7). Two ways of dissolving that are common. The first naturalizes it — illness, hostility, closed roads — so that providence replaces the person of the Spirit. The second inflates it into a template, as though every believer should expect audible vetoes before each decision. The dictionary holds the plain reading against both. The Spirit really and personally directed the apostolic mission, because that mission was foundational and was being steered toward Europe by God Himself. Ordinary guidance since is given chiefly through a sufficient Scripture, a sanctified mind, and the counsel of the church — “the meek will he guide in judgment” (Psa 25:9) — and a Christian who waits for a forbidding before obeying a plain command has mistaken the exceptional for the rule.

The second corruption is closer to home: reading a closed door as a defeat. Paul was barred from a province he plainly wanted, and the bar produced the Macedonian call and the gospel in Europe. Nothing in the narrative suggests he understood it at the time. The believer's confidence is not that he can read the providence while he is inside it, but that the God who writes it is good and cannot be thwarted: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Asia was not refused him for ever — three years in Ephesus were coming. It was refused him then.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Phrugia (G5435), Phrygia; koluo (G2967), to forbid, hinder; dierchomai (G1330), to pass through; episterizo (G1991), to strengthen; horama (G3705), vision.

expand to see more

Greek Phrugia (G5435) — Phrygia; the inland region of Asia Minor.

Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid, hinder, withstand; the Spirit's act in Act 16:6.

Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to go through, traverse; the verb of the apostolic itineraries.

Greek episterizo (G1991) — to confirm, strengthen; the purpose of the third-journey return.

Greek horama (G3705) — vision, sight; the Macedonian man seen in the night at Troas.

Usage

"“Forbidden of the Holy Ghost to preach the word in Asia” — a closed door with a purpose behind it."

"“Strengthening all the disciples” — the apostle goes back to the ground he crossed."

"“Phrygia, and Pamphylia” — the word arrived at Pentecost before the missionary did."
